decks.title: Indifference Curve Analysis — Part 1: Indifference Curves and MRS
goals: Distinguish ordinal from cardinal utility and draw an indifference curve and map from a schedule
Calculate the marginal rate of substitution and explain why it diminishes
Explain the properties of indifference curves, including why they never intersect

slides.heading: Consumer Behaviour: Indifference Curve Analysis
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **ordinal utility**, **indifference curves and maps**, the **marginal rate of substitution** and the **properties** of indifference curves.

visual.alt: Route map of part 1: ranking instead of counting, the indifference schedule, curve and map, the marginal rate of substitution and the properties
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Can you say exactly how many units of satisfaction a mango gives you? Probably not. But you can easily say whether you prefer two mangoes and one banana to one mango and two bananas. This chapter builds a theory of consumer choice on that simple ability to rank. Part one introduces indifference curves and their properties.

slides.heading: Cardinal and ordinal utility
columns: **Ordinal:** utility is only **ranked** — preferred, less preferred or equally preferred.

visual.alt: Table comparing the cardinal approach, which counts utility in utils with a marginal utility schedule, and the ordinal approach, which only ranks bundles using indifference curves

slides.narration: In the cardinal approach we counted utility in utils. The ordinal approach asks for less. The consumer only needs to rank bundles: this one is better, that one is worse, or these two are equally good. Because ranking is more realistic than counting, the indifference curve approach is built on ordinal utility.

slides.heading: The indifference schedule
slides.body_md: An **indifference schedule** lists combinations of two goods that give the consumer the **same satisfaction**.

visual.alt: Ira's indifference schedule: A 1 kg apples and 15 dozen bananas, B 2 and 10, C 3 and 6, D 4 and 3, E 5 and 1
visual.caption: Imagined Dehradun market. Every row gives the same satisfaction.

slides.narration: Meet Ira at a Dehradun fruit market. She is equally happy with any of these five bundles: one kilo of apples with fifteen dozen bananas, two kilos with ten dozen, and so on down to five kilos with one dozen. She does not prefer any bundle to another. A list like this is an indifference schedule.

slides.narration: Plot Ira's bundles with apples on the horizontal axis and bananas on the vertical axis, and join them. The result is an indifference curve. Every point on it gives Ira the same satisfaction. Notice two things about its shape: it slopes downward, and it gets flatter as we move to the right.

slides.heading: Quick check: what is an indifference map?
slides.body_md: Choose the best description of an indifference map.
slides.narration: Remember that one curve shows one level of satisfaction.

slides.heading: The indifference map

visual.alt: Indifference map with three convex curves of the form X times Y equals 8, 18 and 32, labelled IC1, IC2 and IC3 outward from the origin; the curves never meet, and a higher curve shows more satisfaction
visual.caption: Higher curve = higher satisfaction. The curves need not be parallel but never intersect.

slides.narration: A consumer has a whole family of indifference curves, one for each level of satisfaction. Together they form an indifference map. A curve further from the origin contains bundles with more of at least one good, so it shows higher satisfaction. The curves never meet, although they need not be parallel.

slides.heading: Assumptions of the analysis
slides.body_md: Indifference curve analysis rests on these assumptions:

rows: A over B and B over C means A over C
More of a good is preferred to less
She gives up less Y for each extra X

visual.alt: Table of five assumptions of indifference curve analysis: ordinal utility, transitivity, non-satiety, diminishing marginal rate of substitution and given tastes for two goods

slides.narration: The analysis needs a few assumptions. The consumer can rank bundles. Her rankings are consistent, so if she prefers A to B and B to C, she prefers A to C. She prefers more of a good to less. She gives up less of one good for each extra unit of the other. And her tastes do not change.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: calculating MRS
slides.body_md: Find Ira's marginal rate of substitution of apples for bananas at each step.
bullets: Step 1 — **MRSxy = ΔY ÷ ΔX**: bananas given up per extra kilo of apples.
Step 3 — The MRS **falls**: this is diminishing MRS.

visual.alt: Worked example table of Ira's marginal rate of substitution: 5, 4, 3 and 2 dozen bananas per extra kilo of apples
visual.caption: MRS = ΔY ÷ ΔX: it falls at each step.

slides.narration: The marginal rate of substitution measures how many bananas Ira will give up for one more kilo of apples while staying equally happy. From A to B she gives up five dozen. Then four, then three, then two. Each extra kilo of apples is worth fewer bananas to her. This is the principle of diminishing marginal rate of substitution.

visual.caption: Diminishing MRS: the vertical steps shrink as apples increase.

slides.narration: Here the same numbers appear as steps under Ira's curve. Each step across is one kilo of apples. The steps down are five, four, three and two dozen bananas. Because the steps down keep shrinking, the curve gets flatter. That is why a diminishing marginal rate of substitution makes an indifference curve convex to the origin.

slides.heading: Why the MRS diminishes
slides.body_md: As the consumer gets **more X and less Y**, X matters less and Y matters more.

nodes.label: Gives up fewer bananas per kilo

visual.alt: Flow of why the marginal rate of substitution diminishes: more apples weaken the want for apples while scarcer bananas become more precious, so fewer bananas are given up per kilo
visual.caption: Diminishing MRS

slides.narration: Why does the rate fall? As Ira gets more apples, her want for apples becomes weaker. At the same time she has fewer bananas, so each remaining dozen matters more to her. Both forces work together, so she is willing to part with fewer and fewer bananas for each extra kilo of apples.

slides.heading: Properties of indifference curves
slides.body_md: Every indifference curve on a normal map has these properties:

rows: More X must be offset by less Y
More of at least one good
One bundle cannot give two levels

visual.alt: Table of five properties of indifference curves with reasons: downward slope, convexity from diminishing marginal rate of substitution, higher curve higher satisfaction, no intersection, and not necessarily parallel

slides.narration: From the assumptions we get the properties. Indifference curves slope downward, because more of one good must be offset by less of the other. They are convex, because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes. A higher curve means more satisfaction. Two curves never intersect. And they need not be parallel.

visual.caption: Proof by contradiction: this picture cannot describe consistent preferences.

slides.narration: Suppose two curves did cross at A. B is on the first curve and C on the second, directly above B, so C has more of good Y. Ira would be indifferent between A and B, and between A and C, so she would have to be indifferent between B and C. But C has more, so she must prefer it. That contradiction shows the curves cannot cross.

slides.body_md: Must indifference curves be parallel?
slides.narration: Think about what non-intersection actually requires.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: ranking bundles without a map
slides.body_md: A family in an imagined Varanasi colony compares bundles of rice and dal with P (6 kg, 4 kg).
bullets: Step 1 — More of one good and **no less** of the other → **higher** curve.
Step 2 — Less of one and **no more** of the other → **lower** curve.
Step 3 — More of one and **less** of the other → need the **map** to decide.

visual.alt: Worked example table ranking bundles against P with 6 kg rice and 4 kg dal: more of one good and no less of the other is higher; less of one and no more of the other is lower; more of one and less of the other needs the indifference map
visual.caption: Imagined Varanasi family. Non-satiety ranks only some pairs.

slides.narration: Non-satiety lets us rank some bundles without drawing anything. Q has the same rice and more dal than P, so it is on a higher curve. T has more rice and the same dal: also higher. U has less rice and the same dal: lower. But V has more rice and less dal, so only the family's indifference map can tell us.

slides.heading: Quick check: a higher curve
slides.body_md: Where does bundle Q lie compared with P?
slides.narration: Use the idea that more of a good is preferred to less.

slides.heading: Part 1 summary
bullets: Ordinal utility: bundles are ranked, not counted.
An indifference curve joins bundles of equal satisfaction; a map is a set of curves.
MRSxy = ΔY ÷ ΔX and it diminishes, so curves are convex.
Curves slope downward, higher is better, and they never intersect.

rows: Downward, convex, higher is better, never intersect

visual.alt: Summary table of part 1: ordinal utility, indifference curve, marginal rate of substitution and the properties of indifference curves

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The ordinal approach only ranks bundles. An indifference curve joins bundles that give equal satisfaction, and a map is a whole set of such curves. The marginal rate of substitution diminishes, which makes the curves convex. Indifference curves slope downward, higher curves are better, and two curves never intersect.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define MRS with **ΔY ÷ ΔX** and say "at the same level of satisfaction".
Link **diminishing MRS** to **convexity** in every answer on shape.
For non-intersection, draw **A, B, C** and use **transitivity** plus "more is preferred".
Do not say indifference curves must be **parallel** or that their bundles **cost the same**.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. When you define the marginal rate of substitution, mention that satisfaction stays the same. Always connect diminishing marginal rate of substitution with convexity. For the proof that curves cannot cross, label three points and use transitivity with the idea that more is preferred. And remember: the curves need not be parallel, and their bundles need not cost the same.

decks.title: Indifference Curve Analysis — Part 2: Budget Line and Consumer's Equilibrium
goals: Write the budget equation, draw the budget line and find its intercepts and slope

slides.heading: The budget line
slides.body_md:
The **budget line** shows all bundles of two goods that cost exactly the consumer's **whole income**:

**Px·X + Py·Y = M**

nodes.label: Budget line: what she can afford
Move along the line to higher curves
Equilibrium if the curve is convex

visual.alt: Flow of how the consumer reaches equilibrium: she moves along her budget line to higher indifference curves until the line is tangent to a curve and the curve is convex
visual.caption: Two conditions

slides.narration: Put the map and the budget line together. The consumer wants to reach the highest curve she can afford. She keeps moving along her budget line to higher curves until the line just touches a curve. There the slope of the curve, her marginal rate of substitution, equals the slope of the line, the price ratio. And the curve must be convex at that point.

slides.heading: Consumer's equilibrium

visual.alt: Consumer's equilibrium: Meenal's budget line from 24 pens to 12 notebooks is tangent to IC2 (X times Y equals 72) at E, 6 notebooks and 12 pens; it cuts the lower curve IC1 at R and S, and the higher curve IC3 lies wholly beyond it
visual.caption: E: MRS = Px ÷ Py = 2 and IC2 is convex. R and S are on a lower curve; IC3 is unattainable.

slides.narration: Here is Meenal's equilibrium. Her budget line just touches the middle curve at E, six notebooks and twelve pens. At E her marginal rate of substitution equals two, the price ratio, and the curve is convex. The line cuts the lowest curve at R and S, so those bundles give less satisfaction. The highest curve lies beyond her budget.

slides.heading: Why R and S are not equilibrium points
columns: At **R**, MRS **>** Px ÷ Py: she values X more than the market charges — buy **more X**, move down towards E.
At **S**, MRS is **below** Px ÷ Py: she values X less than it costs — buy **less X**, move up towards E.

rows: Px·X + Py·Y = M; slope Px ÷ Py
Tangency: MRS = Px ÷ Py, curve convex
On a lower curve: not equilibrium

visual.alt: Summary table of part 2: budget line and its slope, shifts and rotations, the two equilibrium conditions, and why cutting points are not equilibrium

slides.narration: At R, Meenal values a notebook at more pens than the market asks, so swapping pens for notebooks makes her better off: she moves down the line towards E. At S it is the other way round, so she moves up towards E. Only at E are the two rates equal, and no further swap can raise her satisfaction.

slides.heading: Quick check: cutting points
slides.body_md: Why are cutting points not equilibrium points?
slides.narration: Ask whether she could reach a higher curve without spending more.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Meenal's equilibrium by calculation
slides.body_md: Meenal's curves are X × Y = constant, so her MRS = Y ÷ X.
bullets: Step 1 — Tangency: Y ÷ X = 20 ÷ 10 = 2, so **Y = 2X**.
Step 3 — Check: cost ₹240; MRS = 12 ÷ 6 = 2; the curve is convex.

visual.alt: Worked example table for Meenal's equilibrium: tangency gives Y equal to 2X, the budget gives X equal to 6, so she buys 6 notebooks and 12 pens, costing 240 rupees
visual.caption: Imagined Indore shop; curves X × Y = constant.

slides.narration: We can also find the equilibrium by calculation. For curves like Meenal's, the marginal rate of substitution equals pens divided by notebooks. Setting it equal to the price ratio of two gives pens equal to twice notebooks. Putting that into the budget gives six notebooks and twelve pens. Check the cost, check the ratio, and you are done.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: when the metro fare falls
slides.body_md: Kunal: ₹300; fare falls from ₹30 to ₹20; snacks ₹15. His curves are X × Y = constant.
bullets: Step 1 — Before: Y ÷ X = 2 → **(5 rides, 10 packets)**.
Step 2 — The line rotates out to **15 rides**.
Step 3 — After: Y ÷ X = 20 ÷ 15 → **(7.5 rides, 10 packets)**, on a higher curve.

visual.alt: Worked example table for Kunal: with the fare at 30 rupees his equilibrium is 5 rides and 10 packets; when the fare falls to 20 rupees the line rotates to 15 rides and the equilibrium becomes 7.5 rides and 10 packets
visual.caption: Imagined Guwahati; curves X × Y = constant, MRS = Y ÷ X.

slides.narration: When the fare falls, Kunal's budget line rotates outward. Before, his best bundle was five rides and ten packets. After, the tangency condition gives seven and a half rides and still ten packets. He reaches a higher indifference curve and buys more metro rides. A lower price raises the quantity demanded, just as the law of demand says.

slides.heading: Reaching equilibrium step by step
slides.body_md: Compare the consumer's rate with the market's rate:

visual.alt: Flow of adjustment: if the marginal rate of substitution is greater than the price ratio buy more X; if it is less, buy less X; stop where they are equal
visual.caption: Adjusting towards E

slides.narration: Here is the rule in one picture. If the consumer's marginal rate of substitution is greater than the price ratio, she should buy more of X and less of Y. If it is smaller, she should buy less of X. As she adjusts, her marginal rate of substitution changes until it equals the price ratio, and there she stops.

slides.body_md: Does the consumer spend her whole income at equilibrium?
slides.narration: Think about where the equilibrium point lies.

slides.heading: Part 2 summary
bullets: Budget line: Px·X + Py·Y = M; slope Px ÷ Py.
Income change: parallel shift. One price change: rotation.
Equilibrium: tangency, MRS = Px ÷ Py, with a convex curve.
Cutting points lie on a lower curve; higher curves are unaffordable.

rows: Px·X + Py·Y = M; slope Px ÷ Py
Tangency: MRS = Px ÷ Py, curve convex
On a lower curve: not equilibrium

visual.alt: Summary table of part 2: budget line and its slope, shifts and rotations, the two equilibrium conditions, and why cutting points are not equilibrium

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The budget line shows the bundles that use all income, and its slope is the price ratio. Income changes shift it parallel, and a change in one price rotates it. The consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line touches the highest attainable indifference curve, with the marginal rate of substitution equal to the price ratio and the curve convex.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always label the **intercepts** M ÷ Px and M ÷ Py on a budget line diagram.
State **both** equilibrium conditions; tangency alone is not enough.
Explain **why** cutting points are not equilibrium (MRS ≠ Px ÷ Py).
A **price** change **rotates** the line; an **income** change **shifts** it.
slides.narration: Exam tips for part two. Label both intercepts whenever you draw a budget line. In equilibrium answers, write both conditions: tangency and convexity. Explain why the points where the line cuts a curve are not equilibrium. And remember that a price change rotates the budget line while an income change shifts it.

sections.body_md:
**MRSxy** = amount of Y the consumer gives up for one more unit of X, staying on the **same** indifference curve: **MRSxy = ΔY ÷ ΔX** (absolute slope of the curve).

The fall in MRS as more of one good replaces the other.

sections.heading: 3. Properties of indifference curves
sections.body_md:
1. **Slope downward** — more X must be offset by less Y.
2. **Convex to the origin** — diminishing MRS.
3. **Higher curve, higher satisfaction** — more of at least one good (non-satiety).
4. **Never intersect** — an intersection would make two satisfaction levels equal (proof with points A, B, C and transitivity).
5. **Need not be parallel**, and usually do **not touch the axes** (the consumer wants some of both goods).

sections.heading: 4. The budget line
sections.body_md:
**Budget line:** all bundles that cost exactly the consumer's income: **Px·X + Py·Y = M**. Intercepts **M ÷ Px** and **M ÷ Py**; absolute slope **Px ÷ Py** (the market rate of exchange).

**Budget set:** all bundles costing **M or less** (the triangle under the line). A bundle **inside** leaves income unspent; one **outside** is unaffordable.

key_terms.definition_md: The set of bundles that use up the whole income at given prices.
All bundles that cost no more than the income.

sections.heading: 5. Changes in the budget line
sections.body_md:
- **Income rises (falls):** both intercepts rise (fall) — **parallel** outward (inward) **shift**.

- **Py rises (falls):** y-intercept falls (rises) — line **rotates** on the X-axis, becoming flatter (steeper).
- **Income and both prices change in the same proportion:** no change.

sections.heading: 6. Consumer's equilibrium
sections.body_md:
**Conditions:** (1) **MRSxy = Px ÷ Py** — the budget line is **tangent** to an indifference curve; (2) the curve is **convex** at that point (MRS diminishing).

**Why not elsewhere:** where the line **cuts** a curve, MRS ≠ Px ÷ Py and a move along the line reaches a **higher** curve; curves above the tangency are **unaffordable**. If MRS > Px ÷ Py buy more X; if MRS is below Px ÷ Py buy less X.

The whole income is spent at equilibrium.

key_terms.definition_md: The affordable bundle on the highest attainable indifference curve.
The point where the budget line just touches an indifference curve, so their slopes are equal.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the bundles on an indifference curve cost the same — that describes a **budget line**.
- Writing MRS as ΔX ÷ ΔY, or forgetting "at the same satisfaction".
- Claiming indifference curves must be **parallel**.
- Stating only the tangency condition and leaving out **convexity**.
- Treating a point where the budget line **cuts** a curve as equilibrium.
- Shifting the budget line parallel when only **one price** changes (it rotates).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ / assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: a definition or condition plus a reason or step.
- 3 marks: three points, or a numerical with formula, working and answer.
- 5 marks (and the ISC paper's 4- and 8-mark parts): a labelled diagram with a full explanation of each part.

questions.stem_md: In the indifference curve approach, a consumer is assumed to be able to

options.text_md: measure the utility of each unit in utils
rank combinations of goods in order of preference without measuring utility in numbers
express the utility of every good in rupees exactly
buy unlimited quantities of every good

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** rank combinations of goods in order of preference without measuring utility in numbers. The approach is ordinal: the consumer only says whether she prefers one bundle, the other, or is indifferent. Counting utils and pricing utility in rupees belong to the cardinal approach, and income is always limited.

questions.stem_md: An indifference schedule lists

options.text_md: the quantities of a good bought at different prices
combinations of two goods that cost the same amount of money
the marginal utility of each unit of a single good
combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction. Each row of an indifference schedule is a bundle among which the consumer is indifferent. Price–quantity pairs form a demand schedule, equal-cost bundles lie on a budget line, and MU per unit belongs to cardinal analysis.

questions.stem_md: On an indifference map drawn for a student in an imagined Kochi hostel, a curve lying further from the origin shows

options.text_md: a higher level of satisfaction
a lower level of satisfaction
the same level of satisfaction as every other curve
a higher level of income but the same satisfaction

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a higher level of satisfaction. A higher curve contains bundles with more of at least one good and no less of the other, so (more being preferred to less) it represents a higher level of satisfaction. It says nothing about income; the map shows tastes only.

questions.stem_md: An indifference map is best described as

options.text_md: a single indifference curve with all its points labelled
a diagram of the prices of two goods over time
a set of indifference curves, each showing a different level of satisfaction for the same consumer
a chart of the consumer's income and expenditure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a set of indifference curves, each showing a different level of satisfaction for the same consumer. The map is a family of non-intersecting indifference curves for one consumer, ranked by satisfaction. A single curve shows only one level; prices and income are shown by the budget line, not the map.

questions.stem_md: A Class 12 student in an imagined Shillong school says: "I cannot tell you how many utils a plate of momos gives me, but I know I prefer two plates of momos and one bowl of thukpa to one plate of momos and two bowls of thukpa." Which approach to consumer behaviour does her statement suit?

options.text_md: The cardinal approach, because she names quantities of each good
The law of demand, because she mentions two goods
The ordinal (indifference curve) approach, because she only ranks bundles
Neither approach, because preferences cannot be ranked

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The ordinal (indifference curve) approach, because she only ranks bundles. She cannot measure utility but can rank bundles, which is exactly what the ordinal approach assumes. Naming quantities does not make her statement cardinal; cardinal analysis needs utility in numbers.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Indifference curve analysis does not require utility to be measured in utils.

**Reason (R):** A consumer only needs to rank combinations of goods as preferred, less preferred or equally preferred.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both true; R explains A. Ranking (ordinal comparison) is enough to draw indifference curves, so no cardinal measurement is needed.

questions.stem_md: True or false? All the combinations on one indifference curve of a shopper at an imagined Surat textile market cost the same amount of money.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** An indifference curve joins bundles of equal satisfaction, not equal cost. Bundles of equal cost lie on a budget line; the bundles on one indifference curve usually cost different amounts.

questions.stem_md: A curve joining all combinations of two goods that give a consumer equal satisfaction is called an ___ curve.
questions.solution_md: It is an indifference (iso-utility) curve: the consumer is indifferent among its combinations.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the cardinal and the ordinal measurement of utility, with one illustration of each from a consumer buying fruit at an imagined Nashik market.
questions.solution_md: Contrast counting with ranking, with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Cardinal:** utility is **counted in numbers** (utils), e.g. "a kilo of grapes gives me 30 utils and a kilo of guavas 20 utils".
**Ordinal:** utility is only **ranked**, e.g. "I prefer a kilo of grapes to a kilo of guavas" without saying by how much.

questions.stem_md: Ira's indifference schedule for apples (kg) and bananas (dozen) at an imagined Dehradun market is: (1, 15), (2, 10), (3, 6), (4, 3), (5, 1). Explain how you would draw her indifference curve from it.
questions.solution_md: Plot the combinations and join them; note the shape.

answer.model_answer_md: Plot **apples on the x-axis** and **bananas on the y-axis**; mark each combination as a point (1, 15), (2, 10) … (5, 1); **join the points** with a smooth curve. The curve slopes **downward** and is **convex** because she gives up fewer bananas for each extra kilo of apples.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of an indifference curve and an indifference map, and state what the map tells us about a consumer that a single curve cannot.
questions.solution_md: Define both and say what the map adds: a ranking of all bundles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. An **indifference curve** joins all combinations of two goods that give the consumer the **same satisfaction**.
2. An **indifference map** is a **set of such curves**, each at a different level of satisfaction, with higher curves showing **more satisfaction**.
3. A single curve shows only one level, while the map shows the consumer's **complete scale of preferences**, so we can rank any two bundles.

questions.stem_md: State three assumptions on which indifference curve analysis is based.
questions.solution_md: Any three of the standard assumptions, each briefly explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Ordinal utility:** the consumer can rank bundles but need not measure utility.
2. **Rationality and consistency:** if she prefers A to B and B to C, she prefers A to C (**transitivity**).
3. **Non-satiety and diminishing MRS:** more of a good is preferred to less, and the rate at which she substitutes one good for the other falls as she has more of it.

questions.stem_md: (a) Using Ira's schedule for apples and bananas, (1, 15), (2, 10), (3, 6), (4, 3), (5, 1), describe her indifference curve and explain why she is indifferent among these bundles. (b) Draw (describe) an indifference map with three curves and explain how her satisfaction changes as she moves from one curve to another. (2 + 3)
questions.solution_md: Describe the curve and indifference; then the map with ranking by distance from the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) (2):** plotting the five bundles with apples on the x-axis and bananas on the y-axis gives a **downward-sloping, convex** curve. She is indifferent because each extra kilo of apples exactly **compensates** her for the bananas given up (5, 4, 3, 2 dozen in turn), so every bundle gives the **same satisfaction**.
**(b) (3):** an indifference map has three curves, IC₁ nearest the origin, then IC₂ and IC₃. Every point on **IC₂** has **more of at least one good** than a matching point on IC₁, so it gives **higher satisfaction**; IC₃ is higher still. Moving **outward** from IC₁ to IC₃ means **rising satisfaction**; moving along a curve leaves satisfaction **unchanged**. The curves **never cross**.

marking_scheme.step: Same satisfaction along a curve; no crossing

questions.stem_md: The marginal rate of substitution of X for Y (MRSxy) is the

options.text_md: amount of Y the consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of X while staying equally satisfied
amount of money the consumer pays for one more unit of X
ratio of the price of X to the price of Y set by the market
extra satisfaction from one more unit of X

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** amount of Y the consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of X while staying equally satisfied. MRSxy = ΔY ÷ ΔX along an indifference curve: the Y sacrificed per extra X at constant satisfaction. The price ratio is a market rate shown by the budget line, and extra satisfaction is marginal utility.

questions.stem_md: Suresh, a clerk in an imagined Patna office, is indifferent between 1 cups of tea with 20 packets of biscuits, 2 cups of tea with 14 packets of biscuits, 3 cups of tea with 10 packets of biscuits. What is his MRS of tea for biscuits when he moves from 2 to 3 cups of tea?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 4. MRS = ΔY ÷ ΔX = (14 − 10) ÷ (3 − 2) = 4 packets per cup. 6 is the MRS of the previous step, 10 is the number of packets he keeps, and 2 halves the correct value.

questions.stem_md: Why does the MRS of X for Y fall as a consumer gets more X and less Y along an indifference curve?

options.text_md: The price of X falls as she buys more of it
X becomes less important to her and Y more precious, so she gives up less Y for each extra X
Her income rises along the curve
Y becomes less important to her as she has less of it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** X becomes less important to her and Y more precious, so she gives up less Y for each extra X. With more X its marginal significance falls, and with less Y each remaining unit matters more, so she will part with less Y for each extra X. Prices and income are constant along an indifference curve, and scarcer Y becomes more (not less) important.

questions.stem_md: On an indifference curve, the MRS of X for Y at a point is measured by

options.text_md: the absolute value of the slope of the curve at that point
the distance of the point from the origin
the area under the curve up to that point
the ratio of income to the price of X

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the absolute value of the slope of the curve at that point. MRSxy = −ΔY/ΔX, the (absolute) slope of the curve. Distance from the origin indicates the level of satisfaction, and income divided by price gives a budget-line intercept.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An indifference curve with a diminishing MRS is convex to the origin.

**Reason (R):** Along such a curve the consumer gives up smaller and smaller amounts of Y for each additional unit of X, so the curve becomes flatter.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both true; R explains A. A falling MRS means a falling slope (in absolute terms), which makes the curve bow towards the origin.

questions.stem_md: The rate at which a consumer is willing to substitute one good for another while remaining equally satisfied is called the marginal rate of ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS).

questions.stem_md: On Ira's indifference curve at an imagined Dehradun fruit market, bundle A has 1 kg of apples and 15 dozen bananas and bundle B has 2 kg of apples and 10 dozen bananas. Find her MRS of apples for bananas between A and B.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: MRS = ΔY ÷ ΔX.
Step 2: (15 − 10) ÷ (2 − 1) = 5. So she gives up 5 dozen bananas for one more kilo of apples.

questions.stem_md: Suresh's indifference schedule for tea (cups) and biscuits (packets) at an imagined Patna office ends with the bundles (4, 8) and (5, 7). What is his MRS of tea for biscuits over this last step?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: MRS = ΔY ÷ ΔX.
Step 2: (8 − 7) ÷ (5 − 4) = 1. So 1 packet per cup.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the marginal rate of substitution? Illustrate it with one step of a schedule you construct for a consumer choosing between kites and marbles at an imagined Ahmedabad Uttarayan fair.
questions.solution_md: Define MRS with the formula and give one numerical step.

answer.model_answer_md:
**MRSxy** is the amount of **Y given up** to get **one more unit of X** while staying on the **same indifference curve**: ΔY ÷ ΔX.
Example: moving from (2 kites, 12 marbles) to (3 kites, 8 marbles), MRS of kites for marbles = **4 marbles per kite**.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y diminishes as a consumer moves down an indifference curve.
questions.solution_md: Falling importance of X and rising importance of Y.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. As she gets **more X**, the **intensity of her want for X falls**, so each extra unit of X is worth less to her.
2. As she has **less Y**, each remaining unit of **Y becomes more precious**, so she is willing to give up fewer units of it.

marking_scheme.step: More X: lower intensity of want

questions.stem_md: From Suresh's indifference schedule (tea, biscuits) = (1, 20), (2, 14), (3, 10), (4, 8), (5, 7) at an imagined Patna office, calculate the MRS at each step and comment on the shape of his indifference curve.
questions.solution_md: Compute four MRS values; diminishing MRS gives a convex curve.

answer.model_answer_md:
MRS = ΔY ÷ ΔX at each step: **6, 4, 2, 1** packets of biscuits per extra cup of tea.
The MRS **diminishes** steadily. Because the slope of the curve falls in absolute value as tea increases, the curve becomes **flatter** and is **convex to the origin**.

questions.stem_md: Ira's schedule at an imagined Dehradun market gives the bundles (apples, bananas) (1, 15), (2, 10), (3, 6), (4, 3), (5, 1). Prepare an MRS column and explain what it shows about her preferences.
questions.solution_md: Successive differences in Y over unit changes in X; interpret as diminishing MRS.

answer.model_answer_md:
MRS of apples for bananas: A→B **5**, B→C **4**, C→D **3**, D→E **2** dozen per kg.
It shows that as Ira gets **more apples** she is willing to give up **fewer bananas** for each extra kilo: apples matter less and bananas more to her — the principle of **diminishing MRS**.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the marginal rate of substitution and explain the principle of diminishing MRS with a schedule of your own. (b) Explain why a diminishing MRS makes an indifference curve convex, and what shape the curve would have if the MRS were constant. (3 + 2)
questions.solution_md: Definition, schedule with falling MRS and reason; slope link to convexity and the constant-MRS case.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) (3):** MRSxy is the amount of Y a consumer gives up for one more unit of X while remaining equally satisfied (ΔY ÷ ΔX). Schedule for a student choosing between **notebooks (X)** and **pens (Y)**: (1, 14), (2, 9), (3, 5), (4, 2) — MRS **5, 4, 3**. As notebooks increase, they matter less and pens matter more, so she gives up **fewer pens** per extra notebook: the MRS **diminishes**.
**(b) (2):** MRS is the absolute **slope** of the curve. A falling slope means the curve gets **flatter** as we move right, so it bows towards the origin: **convex**. If the MRS were **constant**, the slope would not change and the curve would be a **straight downward line** (the goods being perfect substitutes).

marking_scheme.step: Constant MRS gives a straight line

questions.stem_md: An indifference curve slopes downward from left to right because

options.text_md: the price of both goods falls along the curve
to get more of one good the consumer must give up some of the other to stay equally satisfied
the consumer's income falls along the curve
both goods become less useful as the consumer gets more of them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** to get more of one good the consumer must give up some of the other to stay equally satisfied. With more X, the consumer can stay at the same satisfaction only if she has less Y, which makes the slope negative. Prices and income do not enter an indifference curve.

questions.stem_md: Two indifference curves of the same consumer cannot intersect because the point of intersection would

options.text_md: lie outside the budget line
make the MRS equal to the price ratio
have to give two different levels of satisfaction at once, which is a contradiction
show that the two goods are complements

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** have to give two different levels of satisfaction at once, which is a contradiction. Each curve stands for one level of satisfaction; a common point would belong to both levels, and with transitivity this implies a bundle with more goods is only as good as one with fewer — a contradiction.

questions.stem_md: A consumer's indifference curve does not touch either axis when she buys tea and coffee at an imagined Coonoor estate shop. Which assumption explains this?

options.text_md: Tea and coffee have the same price
Her income is large enough to buy both
Her MRS is constant along the curve
She always wants some quantity of both goods, so no bundle with zero of one good is on the curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** She always wants some quantity of both goods, so no bundle with zero of one good is on the curve. A curve touching an axis would include a bundle with none of one good; the usual assumption is that the consumer wants some of both. Prices and income do not shape the indifference curve, and a constant MRS would make it a straight line.

questions.stem_md: Bundle P has 6 kg of rice and 4 kg of dal; bundle Q has 6 kg of rice and 5 kg of dal, for a family in an imagined Varanasi colony. If more is preferred to less, Q must lie

options.text_md: on the same indifference curve as P
on a lower indifference curve than P
on the budget line, while P lies inside it
on a higher indifference curve than P

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** on a higher indifference curve than P. Q has the same rice and one more kilo of dal, so (non-satiety) it is preferred to P and lies on a higher indifference curve. Nothing is said about prices or income, so the budget line cannot be judged.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about indifference curves on the same map is correct?

options.text_md: They must be parallel to one another
They intersect at the point of equilibrium
They need not be parallel, but they never intersect
They must all meet the x-axis at the same point

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They need not be parallel, but they never intersect. The curves only have to be non-intersecting; their slopes at a given quantity of X may differ, so they need not be parallel. Equilibrium involves one curve and the budget line, and the curves do not meet the axes.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An indifference curve slopes downward from left to right.

**Reason (R):** Indifference curves on the same map never intersect each other.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true properties, but R does not explain A. The downward slope comes from the need to give up one good to get more of the other at constant satisfaction.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A higher indifference curve represents a higher level of satisfaction.

**Reason (R):** Every bundle on a higher indifference curve costs more money than every bundle on a lower curve.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true (more of at least one good, no less of the other). R is false: cost depends on prices, which the indifference map does not show; a bundle on a higher curve can even cost less than one on a lower curve.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Indifference curves must be parallel to one another because they never intersect.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Non-intersection does not require parallel curves: the curves may come closer or move apart as long as they never cross.

questions.stem_md: Match each property of indifference curves, as drawn for a consumer buying kurtas and dupattas at an imagined Lucknow chikan market, with its reason.

options.text_md: Slopes downward
Convex to the origin
Higher curve, higher satisfaction
Two curves never intersect

match_right.text_md: The marginal rate of substitution diminishes
One bundle cannot give two levels of satisfaction
More of one good must be offset by less of the other
More of at least one good is preferred

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each property follows from an assumption: equal satisfaction (slope), diminishing MRS (convexity), non-satiety (higher curve) and consistency of preferences (no intersection).

questions.stem_md: State any two properties of indifference curves and give the reason for each in one line.
questions.solution_md: Any two properties, each with its reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Downward sloping** — to have more of one good and stay equally satisfied, the consumer must have less of the other.
2. **Convex to the origin** — the MRS of X for Y diminishes as more X is consumed. (Also: never intersect; higher curve, higher satisfaction.)

questions.stem_md: A student at an imagined Pune coaching centre compares bundle P (4 sandwiches, 3 juices) with bundle Q (5 sandwiches, 3 juices). Which bundle lies on a higher indifference curve? Give the reason.
questions.solution_md: Same Y, more X: higher satisfaction by non-satiety.

answer.model_answer_md: **Q** lies on a **higher** indifference curve. It has the **same juices** and **one more sandwich**, and since **more is preferred to less**, Q gives **greater satisfaction** than P, so it cannot be on the same or a lower curve.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: more of one, same of other

questions.stem_md: With the help of a diagram, prove that two indifference curves of the same consumer cannot intersect.
questions.solution_md: Assume an intersection, use transitivity and non-satiety to reach a contradiction.

answer.model_answer_md:
Suppose **IC₁** and **IC₂** cross at **A**. Take **B** on IC₁ and **C** on IC₂ vertically above B, so C has the same X but **more Y** than B.
- A ~ B (both on IC₁) and A ~ C (both on IC₂), so by **transitivity B ~ C**.
- But C has **more Y** than B, so C must be **preferred** to B.
This **contradiction** shows the curves cannot intersect.

marking_scheme.step: Diagram with A, B, C described
Transitivity gives B indifferent to C
Contradiction with more Y in C

questions.stem_md: Explain why an indifference curve is (i) convex to the origin and (ii) does not usually touch either axis. Use the example of a family choosing between milk and curd at an imagined Anand dairy outlet.
questions.solution_md: Diminishing MRS gives convexity; wanting both goods keeps the curve off the axes.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Convex:** as the family gets **more milk**, it gives up **less curd** for each extra litre of milk — the **MRS diminishes** — so the curve becomes flatter and bows towards the origin.
(ii) **Does not touch an axis:** a point on an axis means **zero curd** (or zero milk). The family wants **some of both** goods, so a bundle with none of one good is not on the same curve as bundles with both.

marking_scheme.step: Reason for not touching the axes

questions.stem_md: Explain any four properties of indifference curves. Support one of them with a diagram-based proof. (4 + 1)
questions.solution_md: Four properties with reasons, and one proof.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Slopes downward:** more of X must be matched by less of Y to keep satisfaction constant.
2. **Convex to the origin:** the **MRS of X for Y diminishes**, so the curve flattens as X increases.
3. **Higher curve, higher satisfaction:** a higher curve has bundles with **more of at least one good** and no less of the other.
4. **Never intersect:** a common point would make two different satisfaction levels equal.
**Proof (1):** if IC₁ and IC₂ met at A, a point C on IC₂ directly above B on IC₁ would be **indifferent** to B through A (transitivity) though C has **more Y** — a contradiction.

questions.stem_md: With income M and prices Px and Py, the budget line of a consumer is the set of bundles for which

options.text_md: Px·X + Py·Y is less than M
Px·X + Py·Y = M
X + Y = M
Px ÷ Py = X ÷ Y

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Px·X + Py·Y = M. The budget line shows bundles that cost exactly the whole income. Bundles costing less lie inside it, X + Y = M ignores prices, and the price ratio equals the slope, not X ÷ Y.

questions.stem_md: Meenal in an imagined Indore stationery shop has ₹240; notebooks (X) cost ₹20 each and pens (Y) ₹10 each. What is the slope of her budget line (absolute value)?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 2. Slope = Px ÷ Py = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 (pens given up per notebook). 0.5 inverts the ratio, and 12 and 24 are the intercepts.

questions.stem_md: If a consumer's income rises while the prices of both goods stay the same, her budget line

options.text_md: rotates outward on the x-axis only
shifts outward parallel to itself
shifts inward parallel to itself
becomes steeper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** shifts outward parallel to itself. Both intercepts (M ÷ Px and M ÷ Py) rise in the same proportion and the slope Px ÷ Py is unchanged, so the line shifts outward parallel to the old one.

questions.stem_md: Kunal in an imagined Guwahati has ₹300 for metro rides (X, ₹30) and snack packets (Y, ₹15). If the metro fare falls to ₹20, his budget line

options.text_md: shifts outward parallel, to 15 rides and 30 packets
rotates inward on the y-axis, from 20 to 15 packets
does not change, because income is the same
rotates outward on the x-axis, from 10 to 15 rides, with the y-intercept unchanged at 20

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** rotates outward on the x-axis, from 10 to 15 rides, with the y-intercept unchanged at 20. The x-intercept M ÷ Px rises from 300 ÷ 30 = 10 to 300 ÷ 20 = 15; M ÷ Py stays 20. So the line pivots on the y-axis and becomes flatter (slope 20 ÷ 15). A parallel shift would need a change in income, and the y-intercept depends only on the snack price.

questions.stem_md: With ₹240, notebooks at ₹20 and pens at ₹10, which bundle lies **inside** Meenal's budget line?

options.text_md: 5 notebooks and 10 pens
6 notebooks and 12 pens
8 notebooks and 10 pens
12 notebooks and 2 pens

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 5 notebooks and 10 pens. Costs: (5, 10) = ₹200 (inside); (6, 12) = ₹240 (on the line); (8, 10) = ₹260 and (12, 2) = ₹260 (outside, unaffordable).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a consumer's income rises and both prices stay the same, her budget line becomes steeper.

**Reason (R):** A change in income alters the price ratio Px ÷ Py.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are false. A rise in income raises both intercepts in proportion, so the line shifts outward parallel with the same slope; the price ratio Px ÷ Py depends only on the two prices, not on income.

questions.stem_md: Kunal has ₹300 and a snack packet costs ₹15. How many snack packets can he buy if he spends nothing on metro rides?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: y-intercept = M ÷ Py.
Step 2: 300 ÷ 15 = 20. So 20 packets.

questions.stem_md: Kunal's budget line meets the x-axis at 15 metro rides; a ride costs ₹30. What is his income?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: x-intercept = M ÷ Px, so M = x-intercept × Px.
Step 2: 15 × 30 = 450. So ₹450.

questions.stem_md: A budget line for an imagined Jaipur student has intercepts of 15 movie tickets (X) and 30 ice-cream cones (Y), and her income is ₹300. What is the price of a movie ticket?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Px = M ÷ x-intercept.
Step 2: 300 ÷ 15 = 20. So ₹20.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps for drawing the budget line of a consumer with given income and prices, in the right order.

options.text_md: Join the two intercepts with a straight line
Write the budget equation Px·X + Py·Y = M
Find the y-intercept M ÷ Py (all income on Y)
Find the x-intercept M ÷ Px (all income on X)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Start from the equation, find both intercepts by spending all income on one good, then join them with a straight line.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is a budget line? Write its equation and state what its slope measures.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, equation and the meaning of the slope.

answer.model_answer_md: A **budget line** shows all **combinations of two goods** a consumer can buy by spending her **whole income** at given prices. Equation: **Px·X + Py·Y = M**. Its slope (absolute) **Px ÷ Py** measures the **rate at which the market lets her exchange** Y for X.

marking_scheme.step: Slope as price ratio / market rate of exchange

questions.stem_md: Show the effect on Kunal's budget line (₹300; metro rides ₹30, snack packets ₹15) if the price of a snack packet rises to ₹20.
questions.solution_md: Only the y-intercept changes; the line pivots on the x-axis.

questions.stem_md: Meenal at an imagined Indore stationery shop has ₹240; notebooks cost ₹20 and pens ₹10. Write her budget equation, find the intercepts and the slope, and classify the bundle (8 notebooks, 10 pens).
questions.solution_md: Equation, intercepts, slope, then cost of the bundle against income.

answer.model_answer_md:
Equation: **20X + 10Y = 240**. Intercepts: **12 notebooks** (240 ÷ 20) and **24 pens** (240 ÷ 10). Slope = 20 ÷ 10 = **2** pens per notebook.
(8, 10) costs 8 × 20 + 10 × 10 = **₹260**, more than ₹240, so it lies **outside** the budget line and is **unaffordable**.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with the help of diagrams, how a budget line changes when (i) income falls, prices unchanged; (ii) the price of X falls, income and Py unchanged; (iii) income and both prices double together.
questions.solution_md: Track both intercepts and the slope in each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Income falls:** both intercepts fall in proportion; the line **shifts inward, parallel** to itself (slope unchanged).
(ii) **Px falls:** the x-intercept M ÷ Px rises, the y-intercept is unchanged; the line **rotates outward on the y-axis** and becomes **flatter**.
(iii) **All double:** M ÷ Px, M ÷ Py and Px ÷ Py are all **unchanged**, so the budget line **does not change**.

questions.stem_md: Kunal in an imagined Guwahati has ₹300; metro rides (X) cost ₹30 and snack packets (Y) ₹15. (a) Write his budget equation and describe his budget line and budget set. (b) Show how the line changes if his income rises to ₹450, and separately if the metro fare falls to ₹20. (2 + 3)
questions.solution_md: Equation, intercepts and budget set; then recompute intercepts for each change.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) (2):** **30X + 15Y = 300**. The line joins **10 rides** on the x-axis and **20 packets** on the y-axis, slope **2**. The **budget set** is the triangle formed by the line and the two axes: all bundles costing **₹300 or less**.
**(b) (3):** **Income ₹450:** intercepts become **15 rides** and **30 packets**, slope still 2: a **parallel outward shift**. **Fare ₹20:** the x-intercept rises to **15 rides**, the y-intercept stays **20**: the line **rotates outward on the y-axis** and becomes **flatter** (slope 20 ÷ 15). In both cases his **budget set enlarges**.

Fare fall: rotation with new x-intercept

questions.stem_md: In indifference curve analysis, the consumer is in equilibrium where

options.text_md: the budget line cuts an indifference curve at two points
the indifference curve meets the x-axis
the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve, so MRSxy = Px ÷ Py
MRSxy is greater than Px ÷ Py

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve, so MRSxy = Px ÷ Py. Equilibrium is the tangency of the budget line with the highest reachable indifference curve, where the slopes are equal (MRS = Px ÷ Py) and the curve is convex. Points where the line cuts a curve are on a lower curve.

questions.stem_md: At his present bundle in an imagined Bhopal college canteen, Sameer is willing to give up 4 jalebis for one more samosa, but the market price ratio lets him get a samosa for only 2 jalebis. To raise his satisfaction he should

options.text_md: buy fewer samosas and more jalebis
keep his bundle unchanged
buy more samosas and fewer jalebis until MRS falls to the price ratio
spend less money on both goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** buy more samosas and fewer jalebis until MRS falls to the price ratio. MRS (4) > Px ÷ Py (2): he values a samosa more than the market charges, so swapping jalebis for samosas raises satisfaction. As he gets more samosas, his MRS falls until it equals 2.

questions.stem_md: Tanya at an imagined Nagpur book fair has ₹180; a novel (X) costs ₹15 and a magazine (Y) ₹10. Her indifference curves are of the form X × Y = constant, so her MRS of novels for magazines is Y ÷ X. Which bundle is her equilibrium?

options.text_md: 6 novels and 9 magazines
8 novels and 6 magazines
4 novels and 12 magazines
12 novels and no magazines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 6 novels and 9 magazines. Equilibrium needs MRS = Px ÷ Py = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 and the full budget. At (6, 9): Y ÷ X = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5 and cost = 180. (8, 6) costs ₹180 but MRS = 0.75; (4, 12) costs ₹180 but MRS = 3; (12, 0) is on the axis, outside her curves.

questions.stem_md: Points where a budget line cuts an indifference curve are not equilibrium points because

options.text_md: those bundles are unaffordable
the MRS equals the price ratio there
the consumer is spending less than her income there
the consumer can reach a higher indifference curve by moving along the budget line

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the consumer can reach a higher indifference curve by moving along the budget line. At a cutting point MRS ≠ Px ÷ Py, so moving along the budget line towards the tangency raises satisfaction without extra spending. The cutting points are affordable and on the line (full income spent).

questions.stem_md: Besides MRSxy = Px ÷ Py, the second condition for consumer's equilibrium is that

options.text_md: the budget line is convex to the origin
the indifference curve is convex to the origin at the point of tangency, so MRS is diminishing there
the consumer buys equal quantities of the two goods
the prices of the two goods are equal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the indifference curve is convex to the origin at the point of tangency, so MRS is diminishing there. Tangency alone is not enough: if the curve were concave at the point, the tangency would give minimum, not maximum, satisfaction. The budget line is straight, and equal quantities or prices are not required.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At the point of consumer's equilibrium the slope of the indifference curve equals the slope of the budget line.

**Reason (R):** The consumer's willingness to substitute one good for the other (MRS) must equal the rate at which the market allows her to substitute them (Px ÷ Py).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both true; R explains A. The slope of the indifference curve is MRS and the slope of the budget line is Px ÷ Py; equilibrium needs the two rates to be equal.

questions.stem_md: True or false? At the equilibrium point in indifference curve analysis, the consumer spends her entire income.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The equilibrium lies on the budget line, where Px·X + Py·Y = M, so the whole income is spent.

questions.stem_md: Farhan in an imagined Hyderabad spends ₹200 on bus rides (X, ₹5) and cinema tickets (Y, ₹20). His indifference curves are X × Y = constant, so MRS = Y ÷ X. How many bus rides does he buy in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: MRS = Px ÷ Py gives Y ÷ X = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so X = 4Y.
Step 2: 5X + 20Y = 200 with X = 4Y gives 40Y = 200, Y = 5 and X = 20. So 20 bus rides.

questions.stem_md: Rohit in an imagined Ranchi spends ₹360 on cricket-net sessions (X, ₹30) and swimming-pool tickets (Y, ₹20). His indifference curves are X × Y = constant, so his MRS is Y ÷ X. How many swimming-pool tickets does he buy in equilibrium?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: MRS = Px ÷ Py gives Y ÷ X = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, so Y = 1.5X.
Step 2: 30X + 20(1.5X) = 360 gives 60X = 360, X = 6 and Y = 9. So 9 tickets.

questions.stem_md: State the two conditions of consumer's equilibrium in indifference curve analysis.
questions.solution_md: Tangency (slopes equal) and convexity.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **MRSxy = Px ÷ Py:** the budget line is **tangent** to an indifference curve, so the slopes are equal.
2. **MRS diminishing at that point:** the indifference curve is **convex to the origin** at the point of tangency, so the tangency gives the **highest** attainable satisfaction.

marking_scheme.step: Convexity / diminishing MRS at the point

questions.stem_md: A shopper at an imagined Kolkata New Market finds that her MRS of shirts for trousers is less than the ratio of the price of shirts to the price of trousers. How should she change her purchases, and why?
questions.solution_md: MRS less than the price ratio: substitute away from X until equality.

answer.model_answer_md: She values a shirt at **fewer trousers than the market charges** for it, so she should **buy fewer shirts and more trousers**. As she gives up shirts, her **MRS of shirts for trousers rises** until it **equals the price ratio**, where she is in equilibrium.

marking_scheme.step: MRS rises to the price ratio

questions.stem_md: With the help of a diagram, explain consumer's equilibrium in indifference curve analysis. Show why the points where the budget line cuts a lower indifference curve are not equilibrium points.
questions.solution_md: Tangency at E with both conditions; cutting points can be improved; higher curve out of reach.

answer.model_answer_md:
Draw an **indifference map** (IC₁, IC₂, IC₃) and a **budget line AB**. AB is **tangent to IC₂ at E**: here **MRS = Px ÷ Py** and IC₂ is **convex**, so E is the equilibrium.
AB **cuts IC₁** at R and S. At **R**, MRS > Px ÷ Py, so moving down the line towards E raises satisfaction; at **S**, MRS is below the price ratio, so moving up towards E helps. IC₃ is **unattainable**.

marking_scheme.step: Diagram with map, budget line and tangency E
R and S not equilibrium; IC₃ unattainable

questions.stem_md: Meenal at an imagined Indore stationery shop has ₹240; notebooks (X) cost ₹20 and pens (Y) ₹10. Her indifference curves are X × Y = constant, so MRS = Y ÷ X. Find her equilibrium bundle and check both conditions.
questions.solution_md: Set MRS equal to the price ratio, combine with the budget, then verify.

answer.model_answer_md:
Tangency: **Y ÷ X = 20 ÷ 10 = 2**, so Y = 2X. Budget: 20X + 10(2X) = 240 gives **X = 6**, **Y = 12**.
Check: cost = 6 × 20 + 12 × 10 = **₹240** (whole income); MRS = 12 ÷ 6 = **2** = price ratio; the curves X × Y = constant are **convex**, so (6, 12) is the equilibrium on the curve X × Y = 72.

questions.stem_md: Sameer, at an imagined Bhopal college canteen, would give up 4 jalebis for one more samosa, while the price ratio of samosa to jalebi is 2. His friend says he is "in equilibrium because he is spending all his pocket money". Evaluate the friend's claim.
questions.solution_md: Being on the budget line is necessary but not sufficient; the MRS must equal the price ratio.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **wrong**. Spending all income only puts Sameer **on the budget line**; it is **one** requirement, not the equilibrium itself. Here **MRS (4) > Px ÷ Py (2)**: he values a samosa more than it costs in jalebis, so swapping jalebis for samosas would put him on a **higher indifference curve**. He should buy **more samosas** until his MRS falls to 2.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain consumer's equilibrium in indifference curve analysis with the help of a diagram, stating both conditions. (b) Explain what happens to the equilibrium when the consumer's income increases, prices remaining the same. (3 + 2)
questions.solution_md: Diagram, both conditions and why other points fail; then the income effect on the equilibrium.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) (3):** combine the **indifference map** with the **budget line AB**. The consumer reaches the **highest attainable curve, IC₂**, at the point **E** where AB is **tangent** to it. Conditions: (i) **MRSxy = Px ÷ Py** — the slope of IC₂ equals the slope of AB; (ii) **MRS diminishing** — IC₂ is **convex** at E. Points like R and S, where AB **cuts** a lower curve, give less satisfaction, and a higher curve such as IC₃ is **beyond reach**.
**(b) (2):** a rise in income **shifts the budget line outward, parallel** to AB. It now touches a **higher indifference curve** at a new point **E′**, so the consumer reaches **higher satisfaction**; for normal goods she buys **more of both** goods.

marking_scheme.step: Parallel outward shift of the budget line
New equilibrium on a higher curve

questions.stem_md: Kunal in an imagined Guwahati spends ₹300 on metro rides (X, ₹30) and snack packets (Y, ₹15); his indifference curves are X × Y = constant, so MRS = Y ÷ X. (a) Find his equilibrium bundle. (b) The metro fare falls to ₹20. Find the new equilibrium and explain the change with a diagram. (2 + 3)
questions.solution_md: Tangency with the budget for each set of prices; describe the rotation and the new point.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) (2):** MRS = Px ÷ Py gives Y ÷ X = 30 ÷ 15 = 2, so Y = 2X; 30X + 15(2X) = 300 gives **X = 5, Y = 10**.
**(b) (3):** the budget line **rotates outward on the y-axis**: the x-intercept rises from **10 to 15** rides, the y-intercept stays **20**. New tangency: Y ÷ X = 20 ÷ 15, so Y = (4 ÷ 3)X; 20X + 15 × (4 ÷ 3)X = 300 gives **X = 7.5, Y = 10**. In the diagram the flatter line touches a **higher indifference curve** at the new point. He takes **more metro rides** (5 → 7.5) while snacks stay at 10: a lower price raises the quantity demanded.

marking_scheme.step: Rotation of the budget line described

questions.stem_md:
(i) Neha at an imagined Mysuru silk emporium is indifferent between (1 saree, 9 stoles), (2 sarees, 5 stoles) and (3 sarees, 2 stoles). Calculate her MRS of sarees for stoles at each step and say what shape her indifference curve has. [2]

(ii) Her cousin's schedule shows an MRS that stays at 3 stoles per saree throughout. Explain how the cousin's indifference curve differs and why. [2]
questions.solution_md: Successive ΔY ÷ ΔX and shape; constant MRS gives a straight line.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) MRS = ΔY ÷ ΔX: from the first to the second bundle **4** stoles per saree, then **3**. The MRS **diminishes**, so the curve slopes **downward** and is **convex to the origin**.
(ii) A **constant MRS** means the slope of the curve **never changes**, so the cousin's indifference curve is a **straight downward-sloping line**, not convex. It implies she treats sarees and stoles as **perfect substitutes** at a fixed rate of 3 to 1, which breaks the usual assumption of diminishing MRS.

questions.stem_md:
(i) Aarav in an imagined Chandigarh has ₹360 for badminton court hours (X, ₹30) and shuttlecock boxes (Y, ₹20). Write his budget equation and find both intercepts and the slope. [2]

(ii) Explain why a bundle inside his budget line cannot be his equilibrium, even if it lies on a convex indifference curve. [2]
questions.solution_md: Equation, intercepts and slope; unspent income means a higher curve is reachable.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **30X + 20Y = 360**. Intercepts: **12 court hours** and **18 boxes**; slope (absolute) = 30 ÷ 20 = **1.5**.
(ii) A bundle **inside** the line leaves **part of his income unspent**. With more of a good preferred to less, he could buy **more of one or both goods** and reach a **higher indifference curve** without exceeding his income. So satisfaction is **not maximised** there; equilibrium must lie **on** the budget line, at its tangency with the highest attainable curve.

marking_scheme.step: Higher curve reachable; equilibrium on the line

questions.stem_md:
(i) Using Suresh's indifference schedule at an imagined Patna office — (1 cups of tea, 20 packets of biscuits); (2 cups of tea, 14 packets of biscuits); (3 cups of tea, 10 packets of biscuits); (4 cups of tea, 8 packets of biscuits); (5 cups of tea, 7 packets of biscuits) — calculate the MRS at each step and explain the principle of diminishing MRS and its link with the shape of the curve. [4]

(ii) Explain why indifference curves slope downward and why two indifference curves can never intersect. Use a diagram for the second property. [4]
questions.solution_md: MRS values with the reason and convexity; slope and non-intersection with a diagram-based proof.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) MRS of tea for biscuits = ΔY ÷ ΔX: **6, 4, 2, 1** packets per cup. As Suresh drinks **more tea**, each extra cup matters **less** to him while each remaining packet of biscuits matters **more**, so he gives up **fewer packets** for each extra cup: the **MRS diminishes**. The MRS is the absolute **slope** of the indifference curve, so a falling MRS makes the curve **flatter** as tea increases — the curve is **convex to the origin**.
(ii) **Downward slope:** to keep satisfaction **unchanged**, more tea must be offset by **fewer biscuits**; a rising curve would give more of both goods at the same satisfaction, contradicting non-satiety. **No intersection:** suppose IC₁ and IC₂ cross at **A**. Take **B** on IC₁ and **C** on IC₂ with the **same tea but more biscuits** than B. Since A is indifferent to both B and C, **B and C** must be indifferent (**transitivity**), yet C has **more biscuits**, so C is **preferred** to B. This **contradiction** proves the curves cannot intersect.

questions.stem_md:
(i) Tanya at an imagined Nagpur book fair has ₹180; novels (X) cost ₹15 and magazines (Y) ₹10. Draw (describe) her budget line, and explain how it would change if both prices doubled while her income also doubled. [4]

(ii) Her indifference curves are X × Y = constant (MRS = Y ÷ X). Find her equilibrium bundle and evaluate the suggestion of a friend that she should "buy 8 novels and 6 magazines because that also uses the whole ₹180". [4]
questions.solution_md: Budget line and the all-double case; tangency bundle; compare MRS and satisfaction levels at the friend's bundle.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Budget equation **15X + 10Y = 180**; intercepts **12 novels** and **18 magazines**; slope 15 ÷ 10 = **1.5**. The **budget set** is the triangle under the line. If **income and both prices double**, the intercepts are 360 ÷ 30 = **12** and 360 ÷ 20 = **18** again, and the slope stays **1.5**: the budget line **does not change**, so her choices are unaffected.
(ii) Tangency: **Y ÷ X = 1.5**, so Y = 1.5X; 15X + 10(1.5X) = 180 gives **X = 6, Y = 9**. The friend's bundle (8, 6) does cost **₹180**, so it lies **on** the budget line, but there **MRS = 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75**, which is **below 1.5**: Tanya would gain by giving up novels for magazines. So (8, 6) is a **cutting point** on a **lower** indifference curve (X × Y = 48 against **54** at the equilibrium). The suggestion is **not optimal**: spending all income is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.stem_md: Study the preference survey from an imagined Thrissur school canteen and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined survey, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (a)** P and Q. She is equally happy with P and Q, so they lie on one indifference curve.

**(b)** **Correct option: (b)** a higher indifference curve, because it has one more glass and the same packets. R has the same packets and one more glass than Q, so by non-satiety it is on a higher curve.

**(c) (i)** Transitivity with non-satiety gives a contradiction.

**OR (c) (ii)** Ranking without numbers, needing consistency.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) P and Q

**(b)** (b) a higher indifference curve, because it has one more glass and the same packets

**(c) (i)** P ~ Q and P ~ R would give **Q ~ R** by **transitivity**. But R has **more** than Q and is **preferred** to it. So P could not be on the curve of both Q and R: that would make **two indifference curves meet** at P, which is impossible.

**OR (c) (ii)** Anjali only **ranks** bundles (preferred, indifferent) without giving numbers. The **ordinal approach** needs exactly this information, provided her rankings are **consistent** (transitive).
